messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Imran Khan, a 64-year-old warehouse worker, presents as a man hollowed out by fear. For the past eighteen months, since a business trip to his family’s home region went horribly wrong, he has felt like a prisoner in his own life. The ordeal itself is a memory he fights to keep buried, a fragmented horror of being dragged from his hotel room late one evening. He was held for five days in what he remembers as a damp, earthen pit, a place of total darkness. The worst part was not the hunger or the threats from the men above, but the thing they had thrown in with him on the second day. He never saw it clearly, but he felt it: the dry, slithering weight of a snake moving against his leg in the pitch black. He spent the next three days pressed into a corner, rigid with terror, listening to its movements, certain that at any moment it would strike.

Since his release and return home, the world has become a landscape of hidden threats. The warehouse where he has worked for two decades, once a place of familiar routine, is now a source of constant alarm. The sudden roar of a forklift, the clang of a dropped pallet, or the sight of a coworker walking up behind him in the aisles sends a jolt of panic through his body. He finds himself whipping his head around constantly, checking over his shoulder for a pursuer who is never there. He has come to believe that he is fundamentally unsafe, that a terrible event is always just moments from unfolding, and that there is nothing he can do to stop it. This sense of profound helplessness has settled deep in his bones.

His home, once a sanctuary, offers little relief, especially after sundown. As evening approaches, a familiar dread begins to build. Night-time is the enemy. He cannot tolerate being in a dark room, the blackness pressing in on him, alive with the memory of the pit. Sleep has become something to be evaded at all costs. Most nights, Imran stays in the living room with the lights and television on until he collapses from sheer exhaustion on the couch, desperate to avoid the vulnerability of lying in his own bed in the dark. His wife, Fatima, finds him there in the mornings, his sleep shallow and restless. He often wakes her in the middle of the night, his heart pounding, asking her to check his pulse or feel his forehead. He is constantly scanning his own body for signs of injury or collapse, mistaking the physical symptoms of anxiety for proof of imminent death. He will ask her again and again, "Am I okay? Tell me I'm okay," needing her words to quiet the storm inside him, though the relief they provide is always fleeting.

The triggers are everywhere. He can no longer watch nature documentaries or even flip through magazines for fear of seeing a picture of a snake. When his grandson tried to show him a video on his tablet, Imran flinched back so violently he knocked the device from the boy's hands, an act that left him consumed with shame. The time on the clock turning past 11 PM can bring on a wave of nausea and cold sweat, returning him to the moment his hotel room door was kicked in. He has learned to meticulously avoid these reminders, but the effort is draining. He feels that if he were to allow himself to truly think about what happened, to let the full memory surface, he would not be able to handle it; the thought itself feels like a threat to his sanity. This constant vigilance and avoidance has left him isolated and depleted. The joy has leached out of his life, replaced by a grey, persistent exhaustion. In his darkest moments, he has begun to wonder if a life lived this way is worth living at all. It was this thought, whispered aloud one night to Fatima, that finally brought him to therapy. He is terrified of revisiting the past but is now even more afraid of his future.
